title: The demon nobody saw
translation: Around 1311, word went round that someone had brought a woman from Ise up to the city, and that she had turned into a demon. For about twenty days, people from all over town rushed out every day to see her. "Yesterday she went to the Saionji mansion." "Today she's going to the retired emperor's palace." "Right now she's over at such-and-such." Nobody said they had actually seen her, and nobody said it was a lie. High and low, nobody talked about anything else.

One day I was on my way from Higashiyama over to Agui, and everyone north of Shijō Street was running north. "There's a demon at the corner of Ichijō and Muromachi!" they were shouting. From the Imadegawa river I looked across, and around the retired emperor's viewing stand the crowd was so thick you couldn't get through. So there was something to it after all, I thought, and sent someone to have a look. He didn't find a single person who had actually met her. They kept it up until dark, and in the end fights broke out and there were some ugly scenes.
At the time, a lot of people came down with something for two or three days. Some said that was what the demon story had been about all along: a warning.

literal: Around the Ōchō era, there was talk that (someone) had brought up from the province of Ise a woman who had become a demon, and at that time for about twenty days, every day, the people of the capital and Shirakawa went out in confusion, (saying they were going) to see the demon.
'Yesterday she went to the Saionji; today she will go to the retired emperor's palace. Right now she is at such-and-such a place', they said to each other.
There was no one who said he had really seen her, and no one who said it was a lie.
High and low talked only about the demon and did not stop.
At that time, when I was going from Higashiyama to the area of Agui, the people from Shijō northward were all running toward the north.

'There is a demon at Ichijō and Muromachi!' they were shouting to each other; when I looked from the area of Imadegawa, around the retired emperor's viewing stand they stood so crowded that one could not get through at all.
Thinking 'it seems that, after all, it is not a groundless thing', I sent someone to look, but there was hardly anyone who had met (her).
Until it grew dark they made such a commotion, and in the end quarrels broke out, and there were shocking things.
At that time, generally, there was (a sickness in which) people were ill for two or three days, and there were also people who said, 'That lie about the demon was showing the sign of this.'

notes.text: {応長|おうちやう}: an era name that lasted only about a year, 1311–1312, under Emperor Hanazono. If Kenkō was born around 1283, as is usually assumed, he was in his late twenties. A document of 1313 already calls him a monk; when exactly he took vows is not known.
{鬼|おに}: a demon or ogre. In older stories, a woman can turn into one from jealousy or grief.

The Saionji estate at Kitayama, north-west of the city, the home of Saionji Sanekane (1249–1322), one of the most powerful courtiers of the time. {院|ゐん}: the retired emperor's palace. The 1925 edition says the retired emperor is Go-Uda. Some modern commentaries think instead of Fushimi, who was ruling from retirement at the time.

{安居院|あぐゐ}: a temple in the north of the city, a branch of the Tendai temples on Mount Hiei. Higashiyama is the hill district on the east side of the city. Shijō and Ichijō are the Fourth and First Streets: Kyoto's main east–west streets are numbered from the north, so Kenkō is describing everyone in the northern part of the city.
A viewing stand on First Avenue, built for watching the Kamo Festival procession (see section 137). Imadegawa was a small river that ran nearby.
Contracted from あらざるめり: 'it seems that it is not'. はやく here means 'after all, originally', not 'quickly'. Kenkō admits that for a moment the crowd convinced him too.
{大方|おほかた} … なし: 'hardly anyone, nobody at all'. あふ: 'to meet'. Kenkō's messenger finds a huge crowd and no witness.

き: past for what the writer saw himself. Kenkō was there, and he tells it politely with {侍|はべ}り. ぞ … し: ぞ needs the attributive form, so き becomes し. The last sentence reports what others said, without comment.
